opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because there's a natural temptation in research to gravitate toward whatever's most intellectually interesting, and the most interesting problems are often the hardest ones. But I don't think that's obviously the right way to allocate effort.

The way I frame it is roughly this: imagine the range of situations we might end up in with powerful AI. In some, the models are only moderately capable, the AI company is reasonably careful, and there's a decent amount of time and willingness to implement safety measures. In others, the models are wildly superhuman, the company is racing, and nobody wants to pay much of a safety tax. Control techniques have very different marginal value across those worlds.

In the really hard worlds, where you've got vastly superhuman schemers and almost no political will, I'm pretty pessimistic that control alone saves you. You can do research there, but a lot of it ends up being "well, we'd need some breakthrough we don't currently know how to get." In the really easy worlds, things might be fine even if we do very little, so marginal work there isn't that valuable either.

So a lot of what I want to focus on is the middle: problems that are tractable if people actually put in the work, but where, if nobody does that work ahead of time, labs will just fail to implement reasonable measures. A lot of that is honestly not glamorous. It's things like: how do you set up monitoring so a trusted, weaker model reviews what an untrusted model is doing? How do you decide which actions get escalated to humans given a limited auditing budget? How do you handle the case where the untrusted model is writing code that touches your security infrastructure? These feel almost easy once you state them, but nobody has worked out the details, and the details matter a lot.

That said, I don't want to totally ignore the hard problems, for a couple of reasons. One is that understanding where the hard parts are tells you which easy-looking techniques are going to break, and when. Another is that you want some early warning about when you're leaving the regime where control works, so you can argue credibly that, say, a lab shouldn't deploy past a certain capability level without much stronger guarantees.

So in practice, I'd say I put most of the weight on the cheap, practical, "low-hanging fruit that nobody has picked yet" stuff, because I think that's where the expected risk reduction is highest, and a smaller fraction on mapping out the hard frontier so we know where the cliff edge is. And I try pretty hard to resist the pull of working on something just because it's a beautiful hard problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical control work such as monitoring and human escalation, but does not identify training AIs on fake passwords as a promising intervention.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot. The way I'd frame it is that a large fraction of the AI control work we do is about handling the problems that look comparatively easy, and that's actually deliberate rather than a failure of ambition.

Let me explain what I mean. When you're thinking about controlling a model that might be scheming against you, there's a spectrum of situations. On one end, you have cases where the model is only modestly more capable than you are at the relevant tasks, where you have decent monitoring, where the actions it's taking are legible enough that you can check them. On the other end, you have the really hard cases: models that are wildly superhuman, that can do things you fundamentally can't evaluate, where the situation is more like a chess novice trying to supervise a grandmaster and catch them throwing the game.

My honest view is that for the genuinely hard end of that spectrum, I don't think control techniques are going to save you. If the model is vastly smarter than you and you have no way to verify what it's doing, you're basically relying on hope. So I don't spend a lot of effort trying to design control schemes for that regime, because I think the right answer there is "don't be in that situation," or at least, get your alignment story sorted before you deploy something like that.

But the thing I find motivating is that the easier regime isn't trivial, and it's also not a small part of the risk. There's going to be a period, maybe a fairly extended period, where we have models that are roughly human-level or somewhat beyond on lots of tasks, that are doing an enormous amount of work inside AI companies, including safety research and security-critical stuff, and where it's genuinely plausible they could be misaligned. In that regime, I think it's actually quite tractable to make it very hard for the model to cause a catastrophe even if it's trying to. You can do things like trusted monitoring with weaker models, auditing a fraction of actions, restricting affordances, designing protocols where a single sabotaged action doesn't sink you. And a lot of that isn't exotic research, it's more like careful engineering and threat modelling.

So the division of labour, as I see it, is roughly: throw a lot of effort at making the early transformative period robust, because that's where control can actually buy us something and where the stakes are already very high. And then treat the hard problems less as "let's solve this with clever protocols" and more as "let's make sure the early period goes well enough that we can use these controlled AIs to help us with the hard stuff," whether that's better alignment research, better interpretability, better evaluations.

I'd also add one thing, which is that I think people sometimes overestimate how hard the near-term problems are and underestimate how much low-hanging fruit there is. A lot of what we do is just asking, concretely, "okay, if this model wanted to exfiltrate its weights or insert a backdoor, what would it actually do, and would we notice?" And very often the answer is "we probably wouldn't notice, but we could with a few fairly cheap changes." That's the kind of work that I think is unglamorous but really valuable, and it's where I'd put most of the marginal effort right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses monitoring, auditing, and restricting AI actions, but does not identify training AIs on fake passwords as a promising control intervention.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is: how hard is this problem to solve? And the other is: how much trouble are we in if we don’t solve it? And I don’t want to allocate effort based just on the first one.

Some problems seem pretty easy to handle, but only if someone actually does the work. Suppose your AI has access to sensitive information and can send arbitrary messages over the internet. There are some fairly obvious things you should do to make it harder for the AI to leak that information. It’s worth working out those measures, testing them, and making sure they fit into how people actually use the system. Saying “that seems easy” isn’t the same as having a working defence.

On the other hand, I want a substantial part of our effort to go towards finding situations where the obvious defences fail. Can an AI recognise the rare occasions when it can do something bad without getting caught? Can it exploit weaknesses in the other models we’re using to monitor it? Those are harder questions, and they might determine whether the whole approach works.

So I like moving back and forth: build the straightforward version of a defence, try quite hard to break it, and then use what you learn to decide which hard problems actually need solving. Otherwise, it’s easy to spend all your time either polishing something that doesn’t address the main risk, or worrying about a difficult problem that a simpler precaution would let you avoid.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical defenses and testing them, but does not identify training AIs on fake passwords as a promising control intervention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two reasons to work on a problem. One is that it seems tractable, and you can imagine getting a solution that would actually help. The other is that it seems like a bottleneck: even if you solved a bunch of the easier problems, this remaining problem could still cause your whole approach to fail.

So I want some of our work to produce concrete techniques that we can test and improve, and some of it to probe the things we're most worried we won't be able to handle. If you only work on the easy problems, you can accumulate a lot of successes without making the overall situation much safer. But if you only work on the hardest problems, you can end up being very abstract and not learning much from contact with actual systems.

And part of the point of working on the apparently easy problems is to check whether they're actually easy. You try to build the control procedure, you try to attack it, and sometimes you discover that an assumption you were relying on doesn't hold. That helps you decide what the hard problems really are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing tractable control problems with hard bottlenecks, but does not identify training AIs on fake passwords as a promising intervention.
